Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3plr90$m...@news.gate.net>, Kelly <du...@gate.net> wrote:
>Hello...I was just wondering...could a haven uncovered be played on one
>of your own vampires. Say could I put fame on Smudge...then haven
>uncovered on him next turn would it be legal to attack my own vampire then?
>Any light you can shed on this subject would be greatly appreciated.THanks:)

Well, there's no prohibition against putting it on your own
vampire. However, the question then becomes whether or not you can
attack yourself. There have been lots of haggles over the official
rules, but no clear decision. The best I can tell you is that we
usually play by the rule that you can't make a (D) attack against one of
your own minions. It makes things a lot more clear and seems to us to
be quite in the spirit of the rules.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Cards with directed actions, other than bleed cards, may be directed
against yourself unless the card indicates otherwise.

Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3ps7m5$3...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>,

Thomas R Wylie <aa...@cats.ucsc.edu> wrote:
>Cards with directed actions, other than bleed cards, may be directed
>against yourself unless the card indicates otherwise.

Why? In the rules, (D) is defined as against someone else. And
besides, this leads to one of the cheesiest combos in the game (taking a
(D) against your own Famous Vampire). So both from a rules reading and
a game balance perspective, it makes *much* more sense to not allow it.
Which leaves me only one question: Why did you rule on this in this
manner?

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Joseph Cochran <js...@discus.ise.vt.edu> wrote:
> Why? In the rules, (D) is defined as against someone else. And
>besides, this leads to one of the cheesiest combos in the game (taking a
>(D) against your own Famous Vampire). So both from a rules reading and
>a game balance perspective, it makes *much* more sense to not allow it.
>Which leaves me only one question: Why did you rule on this in this
>manner?

Looking the corrected rulebook, I can't find anything that says you can't
use D actions on yourself ("Directed actions... allow you to direct the
action against *any* Methuselah", Section 13.3.1). Matt Burke just confirmed
that you can use D actions against yourself, with the exceptions being any
kind of bleed, and any card that explicitly says it's used on another
Methuselah. There may be certain cards which would be better off if you
couldn't use them against yourself (e.g. Haven Uncovered), but in general
it's not a problem.



Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3q2ip1$r...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>,

Thomas R Wylie <aa...@cats.ucsc.edu> wrote:

>Looking the corrected rulebook, I can't find anything that says you can't
>use D actions on yourself ("Directed actions... allow you to direct the
>action against *any* Methuselah", Section 13.3.1). Matt Burke just confirmed
>that you can use D actions against yourself, with the exceptions being any
>kind of bleed, and any card that explicitly says it's used on another
>Methuselah. There may be certain cards which would be better off if you
>couldn't use them against yourself (e.g. Haven Uncovered), but in general
>it's not a problem.

Be careful with your logic here. If you can't bleed yourself
because of, I guess, the definition in 12.3.1 Minion Actions under the
Bleed definition ("It is the basic action of your minion to undermine
the power and influence of another player ... meddling directly in the
affairs of another Methuselah."), then you can also use that same logic
to apply the first definition of directed action to what you cannot do
("Actions that directly affect another Methuselah are called directed
actions and can only be blocked by that Methuselah's minions. Other
actions are called non-directed..." 13.3.1, second and third sentence).
By the logic that you can't bleed yourself because of the rule
in the book (quoted above), you can't direct an action against yourself,
since (by the parallel wording) you are not *another* Methuselah. And
if an action is not directed against another Methuselah, it's
non-directed. So to keep a directed action directed, it *must* be done
against another Methuselah, and thus cannot be done against yourself.
The later section saying that you can direct against *any* Meth. doesn't
have to be exclusive of the first paragraph. Simply take the union of
the two sets, <another Meth> and <any Meth>, and you come up with being
able to direct the action at any other Methuselah.
That's the theory, and it works much better than saying "and the
cards that this rule *does* break aren't a problem."


